transcript.text: Hi Shannon — how are you settling into your new flat?
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Really well, thanks.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: You look like you're going shopping.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Yes, I am.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: My cousins are coming to stay for a couple of days, and I have to cook for them.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Well, there are plenty of places to buy food in Kite Place — it's the area by the harbour.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Oh, OK, I'll find that on the map.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: What sort of food do you need to get?
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Well, neither of them eats meat but they both like fish.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Well, there's a really good fish market there.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Oh great — where is it exactly?
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: It's at the far end of Kite Place, so you have to go over the bridge and then it's on the right.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: OK — is it open all day?
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: It doesn't close until four, but I'd recommend going earlier than that — it does run out of some things.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Oh, I don't want that to happen.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: As long as you get there by 3.30, you should be fine.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: It's only 11 now, so plenty of time.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Do you need to buy vegetables too?
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: I do, and I want to avoid all the plastic packaging in the supermarket!
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Well, there's a really nice organic shop there.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Now what's it called ... it's the name of a flower.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: I know, it's 'Rose'.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: That's a nice name.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Yeah — it sells vegetables and quite a lot of other stuff.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: And where's that?
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Well, as you reach the market, you'll see a big grey building on your left — I think it used to be a warehouse.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Anyway, now it's a restaurant upstairs, but the ground floor has two shops either side of the entrance and it's the one on the left.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: That's easy enough.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: You can't miss it — there's also a big sign on the pavement so you can look for that.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Fine!
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: I guess if I need anything else, I'll have to go to the supermarket.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Yeah — you should be able to get everything you need, but there's a minibus that goes to the supermarket if you need it.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: It's purple and the number is 289.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Thanks, that's great.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: So what do you need to get at the fish market?
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: The salmon is always very good and the shellfish.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: I'm going to make a curry, I think, and I need about 12 prawns for that.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: They'll have plenty of those.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Have you ever tried samphire?
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: No — what's that?
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: It's a type of seaweed.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: I just ask for a handful and you fry it in butter.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: It's delicious!
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Oh, I might try that — how do you spell it?
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: It's S-A-M-P-H-I-R-E.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Great — it's always good to try something different.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: I'll see what beans they have in the organic shop and I think I'll get something for dessert there.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: How about a mango?
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: I'm not sure — they're not always ripe.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: I'd prefer a melon — it's bigger too.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Good idea.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: The owner also sells a lot of spices there that you can put in a curry, and things like coconut.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Oh, that's very helpful.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: I'll have a look.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: No problem.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: I know bread doesn't really go with curry but I always like to have some in case.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: As I said — all the bread is home-made and there's lots of variety.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: I like the brown bread myself.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Mm, sounds good.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: They sell other things there too.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Like cakes?
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: I love chocolate cake.
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: Well — not that, but they have a whole range of tarts and the best are the strawberry ones.
transcript.speaker: LEON

transcript.text: Perfect — hopefully I won't even have to go to the supermarket!
transcript.speaker: SHANNON

transcript.text: The children's book festival is coming up again soon and here to tell us all about it is the festival's organiser, Jenny Morgan.
transcript.speaker: PRESENTER

transcript.text: So tell us what we can expect this year, Jenny.
transcript.speaker: PRESENTER

transcript.text: Well, as usual we've got five days of action-packed exciting events for children, with writers coming from all over the country getting involved.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: Just to give you an idea of what's on offer in the workshops, first of all, there's a very special event called Superheroes.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: This is a chance for deaf children to share their reading experiences with author Madeleine Gordon, who is herself hearing impaired. 'Just do it' is a practical workshop led by the well-known illustrator Mark Keane.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: He'll take participants on a magical journey to faraway lands with an opportunity for aspiring actors to do some role play. 'Count on me' is an inspiring and entertaining look at the issues of friendship for 13—14-year-olds.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: It looks at some of the friendships described in popular books and asks participants to compare these with their own experiences. 'Speak up' is part of a series of workshops on the subject of mental health.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: This is a creative writing workshop encouraging children to describe situations where young people experience loneliness.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: A recent survey revealed that children can be lonely even when they're at home with their families. 'Jump for joy', as many of you will know, is the heart-warming, best-selling story by Nina Karan about a young girl's trip to visit her relatives in India.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: It recently received the gold medal at the Waterford Awards.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: Nina will get children to celebrate the word 'joy' by writing a poem. 'Sticks and stones' is the beautifully illustrated picture book for young readers about a community who organise an African-Caribbean festival to help local children learn about their Jamaican roots.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: This will be a musical event where children will have the chance to play steel drums.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: This is bound to be very popular, so please book as soon as possible.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: Thanks Jenny.
transcript.speaker: PRESENTER

transcript.text: That all sounds really interesting.
transcript.speaker: PRESENTER

transcript.text: I'm just wondering if you have a favourite book you could recommend for our readers?
transcript.speaker: PRESENTER

transcript.text: It's hard to choose, but Alive and Kicking is definitely worth mentioning.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: You won't have heard of the writer as it's her first book — which is really impressive.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: It's basically the teenage diary of a boy from Somalia who comes to live in the UK.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: It deals with the serious issue of immigration and all the challenges the boy has to face at school and with the language barrier, etc.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: Usually, books like this are quite sad, but this one actually made me cry with laughter.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: On each page, there are simple but hilarious black and white stick drawings of the boy with his friends and teachers.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: At the end of each diary entry, there are new English words the boy learns each day, which may help develop some children's vocabulary.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: I think my kids would enjoy that.
transcript.speaker: PRESENTER

transcript.text: What about any advice for parents on how to encourage their children to read more?
transcript.speaker: PRESENTER

transcript.text: Well, this is something I get asked about a lot.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: There are so many distractions for kids these days that it can be hard to find time for reading.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: One thing I'd say is to make time to sit down with your child and share books with them.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: A lot of parents give up reading aloud to their children as soon as they learn to read independently, but this is a mistake.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: It's good to read more advanced books to them as it helps to develop their vocabulary If you don't have time for this, then let them listen to audio books.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: Often, they'll want to read books they've listened to for themselves.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: I think it's a good idea to make a mental note of the type of books your child is reading — often they just read the same genre all the time, which can get a bit boring.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: You can introduce new authors and genres to them.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: Librarians should be able to help you with this.
transcript.speaker: JENNY

transcript.text: Well Jenny, I think that's really useful.
transcript.speaker: PRESENTER

transcript.text: Hi Jake.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: How are you getting on with the practical teaching?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: It's harder than I expected, but I've got some great classes.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: How about you?
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Not brilliant.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: I'm really struggling with my Year 12 science class.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Are they hard to control?
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Well, I don't have discipline problems as such.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: It's just that they don't seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: It's depressing.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: They listen to what I say, and I gave them a test last week and the results weren't too bad, but there's no real engagement.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: I was wondering about something on the children's diets ... you know, asking them to record what they eat and maybe linking it to their state of health.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Mmm.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Let's think.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: OK, but you'd also need to have access to the children's medical records and I don't think people would be happy about that; confidentiality would be an issue.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it's not going to be easy.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Wouldn't that be upsetting for the children?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Well, the animals don't have to be harmed in any way.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: It could just be an experiment where they're given a certain diet and the effects are observed.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Would I have to get permission to use animals?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Yes, you'd have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form, but it's quite straightforward.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: But if we found out that, say, a particular diet affects the health of animals, the same thing wouldn't necessarily be true for people. would it?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: No that's true, but the findings for any experiment are going to be limited.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: It's inevitable.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: I suppose so.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: So what animals could I use to investigate the effects of diet?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Mice?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: You'd need experimental mice — ones that have been specially bred for experiments.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Well, something to do with nutrition.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: So maybe we could look at food supplements ... things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Mmm.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: That might be rather broad.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Maybe just look at the effects of one supplement, like sugar, on the health of the mice?
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar, that they don't really need?
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Do they eat it or do they decide to leave it?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Then later on, you could do a follow-up experiment adding another variable.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Like, you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active. running on a wheel or something, and the others just sit around and don't do much.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Or I could repeat the experiment but change the type of food I provided . or use mice with a different genetic structure.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: But I think your idea would be more interesting, I might think about that some more.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: So can I talk through a possible procedure for the experiment where mice are given a sugar supplement?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: I did a similar experiment in college actually.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: So how many mice would I need?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: I'd say about 12.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: And all young ones. not a mixture of old and young.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: And I'd need two groups of equal sizes, so six in each group.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: And how would I tell them apart?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: I suppose I could put some sort of tag on one group ... or just mark them in some way?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: You could use food colouring, that wouldn't hurt them.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Perfect.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Then each group would go into a separate cage, and one group, let's call them group A, would be the control group.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: So they'd just have ordinary mouse food.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: I suppose you can buy that?
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Yes, it comes in dry pellets.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: And the other group would have the same as the first group, but they'd also have the extra sugar.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Would you just give them straight sugar?
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: It might be better to give them something like cereal with it.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Mmm.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: Then you'd need to weigh the mice, I should think once a week.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: And you'd need an electronic balance.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: But we can't hold them on the balance, or it'd affect the reading.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: So you need something called a weighing chamber to stop the mice from running away.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: It sounds complicated, but actually you can just use a plastic box with holes in the top.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: So once we've measured the weight gain of each mouse we can work out the average for each group. as well as the standard deviation.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: And then see where we go from there.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: That sounds cool, I think the students will enjoy it.
transcript.speaker: CLARE

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.speaker: JAKE

transcript.text: In today's lecture, I'm going to be talking about microplastics.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres in size.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: Recently there's been a greater awareness that there are large quantities of plastic waste — big and small — in the environment.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: The amount of plastic waste in the oceans has received widespread attention, but far less is known about the effects of microplastics in freshwater and particularly in soil.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: Microplastics can enter the environment via a number of different sources.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: Threads and microfibres detach from synthetic clothing every time they're put in a washing machine, and these find their way into the water system.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: Other sources include big pieces of plastic waste that are already in the environment, and these break down into microscopic particles over a period of time.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: On a larger scale, factory waste is another route, as are tyres which wear down as cars, lorries and so on travel along road surfaces.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: We already understand some of the impacts of microplastics from studies involving fish and other animals.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: There is evidence that microplastics harm small creatures in a variety of ways, such as by damaging their mouths, or by impairing their ability to feed, for example when microplastics get lodged in their digestive system.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: Surprisingly perhaps, it is likely that humans consume microplastics, as these have been detected in a wide range of food and drink products, including bottled water, as well as in water that comes direct from the tap.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: What's more, salt and many kinds of seafood have also been found to contain microplastics.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: However, it's important to underline that there is not yet conclusive proof that microplastics cause significant harm to people.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: In many countries, including here in the UK, there is legislation which prevents manufacturers from adding plastic microbeads to shower gels. facial cleansers and toothpaste.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: It is very difficult to accurately estimate the total amount of microplastic particles in the soil as they can be hard to detect, but we do know they are carried in the air and deposited in the soil by rain.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: What's more, many of the fertilisers used by both farmers and gardeners contain microplastics.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: A team from the Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge has carried out a study of the effects of microplastics on the digestive tracts of earthworms.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: These worms, which live in topsoil, are an essential component of our agricultural system.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: By feeding on soil, they mix nutrients into it, thereby making it more fertile.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: The researchers set out to discover whether the introduction of microplastics into the soil — and the subsequent ingestion of these by earthworms — would impact soil quality and ultimately inhibit plant growth.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: The short answer was, yes, it did.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: After placing three different types of microplastic particles into the soil, they planted perennial rye grass.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: The particles of microplastic, which included biodegradable PLA and conventional high-density polyethylene, or HDPE, were then ingested by the earthworms in the soil.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: The result was that the worms lost weight rapidly.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: What's more, a lower percentage than normal of the rye grass seeds germinated, and the researchers concluded that this was a direct result of the earthworms being unable to fulfil their normal role in making soil more fertile.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: The team also discovered that there was an increase in the amount of acid found in the soil. and this was attributed mainly to the microplastic particles from conventional HDPE plastic.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: The conclusions of the study make for very interesting reading — I've included the reference in the notes to give you at the end of this session.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: To summarise, the authors proposed the idea that we need to regard soil as we would regard any other process in nature.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: This means we should accept the implications of soil being dependent on decaying and dead matter constantly being passed through the bodies of earthworms.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER

transcript.text: That is, when soil becomes impoverished by the presence of microplastics, not only ecosystems but also the whole of society are negatively impacted.
transcript.speaker: SPEAKER
